$comment: Which external document each citation in a normative artifact means, and whether anyone can consult it. Normative for what IAES may cite: a claim about a document nobody can open is a claim nobody can check. It says nothing about whether a document supports what IAES attributes to it -- that is a separate question this file deliberately does not answer.

two_questions.identity: Does the citation name a document? A number alone identifies an IETF RFC, because a revision gets a new number. It does not identify an ISO standard, which is revised under the same number, so an ISO citation without an edition names a family.
two_questions.availability: Given an identified document, can it be consulted? This can only be asked once identity is settled -- which is why `unresolved` exists and is not a kind of `unavailable`.

vocabulary.public: Published without charge by its publisher. Anyone can consult the same text.
vocabulary.available: Not public, and a copy is held. Requires edition, language and access_basis.
vocabulary.unavailable: Identified, not public, and no copy held. Checking a claim about it needs a purchase.
vocabulary.unresolved: The citation does not identify a document. Availability cannot be asked yet. Requires a note saying what would resolve it.

references.note: Not a prose citation. Every schema declares this dialect in `$schema`, so the schemas depend on its specification as surely as the text depends on the documents it names. Identified by URI, which pins the draft.

Cited without an edition in GOVERNANCE.md, IAES_SPEC.md and two schemas, so it names a family rather than a document. The 2016 English edition is held, and the claims were probably made against it -- but nobody recorded that, which is precisely the gap. Resolved by pinning the edition in each citation.
Cited without an edition. The 2018 English edition is held. Resolved by pinning it in the citation.
Cited without an edition. The copy held is the 2024 Spanish edition; clause numbering can differ between translations, so an edition and a language are both needed before a clause is cited from it.

Cited without an edition and no copy is held. Recording it as unavailable would answer a question that cannot be asked: without an edition there is no document to be unavailable. The code list is widely mirrored, which is not the same as the standard being identified.
Names a part but no edition, and no copy is held. rfc/IAES-RFC-002.md proposes withdrawing the attribution rather than pinning it, because it was never verified.
Names a part but no edition. The 2015 English edition is held and was read on 2026-09-06; rfc/IAES-RFC-002.md proposes withdrawing the attribution because that reading did not support it.

Cited as a series on purpose: the citations cover at least two different subjects -- health status levels and a six-block processing model -- which cannot both be one part. A series names no document, so availability cannot be asked at all.
Identified -- the citation pins the edition -- and no copy is held. Cited in GOVERNANCE.md as precedent for a normative annex, so a claim about it would need the document.

mentions_not_dependencies.$comment: Named by a normative artifact and depended on by nothing. Recorded rather than filtered, so that 'we did not register it' is a decision somebody made and not an omission nobody noticed.
mentions_not_dependencies.ISO 8601: Named only to explain what RFC 3339 profiles, and to record that an earlier version of this specification cited it in RFC 3339's place. Nothing depends on it: the schemas use JSON Schema's date-time and date formats, which are defined by RFC 3339.
mentions_not_dependencies.ISO 13374: Appears in the version history describing what release 1.2 did, and in prose explaining why the current citations say `series`. Neither is a dependency of this release.

held_but_not_cited.$comment: Documents the editor holds that no normative artifact cites. Recorded so 'we have it' is never confused with 'we use it', and so a future citation knows an edition is already available.
